questions.question: Who is the narrator?
choices: the real author in every case
the voice that tells the story

questions.question: Which pronouns commonly signal first-person narration?
A narrator refers to the protagonist as “she” and reports only what she notices. Which point of view is this?
A narrator reports the thoughts of several characters in different scenes. Which point of view is most likely used?
A recipe says, “You stir the mixture until smooth.” Which point of view is used?
A narrator tells events as “I,” but is a witness rather than the central character. What is this narrator?
A narrator knows only one character’s private thoughts. What limits the reader’s access?
A narrator describes several characters’ private thoughts and pasts. What kind of access does the narrator have?
The narrator says, “I knew the bridge was unsafe, but I crossed anyway.” Which detail signals first person?
choices: the event happens in the past

questions.question: Readers learn only what a frightened child sees in a dark hallway. How does this viewpoint shape suspense?
choices: it proves the author is frightened

questions.question: A narrator claims “nothing unusual happened,” while describing a door opening by itself. What might readers question?
A first-person narrator describes another character’s actions but cannot know that character’s unspoken thoughts. Why?
choices: the narrator’s knowledge is limited to what can be observed or inferred

questions.question: Two narrators describe the same argument differently. What can comparing them reveal?
choices: that the event did not happen

questions.question: A narrator calls a rival “careless,” but the rival’s actions show careful planning. What should readers consider?
choices: whether the setting is first person
whether the narrator’s judgment is biased
whether the plot has a climax
whether the rival is the author

questions.question: A text addresses the reader as “you” and places the reader in a sequence of choices. What effect can this have?
choices: it can make the reader feel directly involved
it changes the text to first person

questions.question: An outside narrator reports visible actions without stating anyone’s thoughts. What is the narration closest to?
The narrator knows the coach’s plan but not the player’s thoughts. What can readers infer about narrative access?
choices: the narrator must be first person
the narrator’s access may be selective or shifting
the story has no point of view

questions.question: A student says “the narrator is the author” because both use “I.” What is the best correction?
choices: authors cannot write in first person
a first-person narrator is a created voice and may differ from the author
narrators have no role in fiction

questions.question: A narrator describes a friend as “honest,” though the friend repeatedly hides important facts. What creates doubt?
choices: the gap between the narrator’s claim and the evidence

questions.question: A third-person narrator follows one character closely, then reveals another’s hidden thought in a later chapter. What is a careful conclusion?
choices: the setting changes point of view
the narrative access expands or shifts
